segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: Good afternoon, everyone. I am pleased to be here with you this afternoon, and especially to be among all of you young people.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: Today, if they do the average of our ages, they'll be a lot younger than I am today. So today, we'll do a lot of averages about how old we are. I want to thank, first of all, the YouthConnekt Africa Hub, which has convened this 2026 summit here in Kigali.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: And also to thank you, YouthConnekt Africa Hub, for choosing to partner with the African School of Governance, particularly to deliver this afternoon's session. Honorable ministers, excellencies, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen, I want to begin by recognizing all the young people participating in this YouthConnekt Africa Summit 2026, particularly all of you who have chosen a career in public service. Many of you also have chosen a career in civil service, different types.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: But you are also entrepreneurs, entrepreneurs who are employing yourselves, but providing jobs to many others as well. I want to thank you for the initiative that you have taken to do that. I want to invite you, all of you this afternoon, to join me in exploring the theme that we have been given about this session this afternoon together.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: Our theme is about passing the torch. When you think about it, it's a very vividly active process. And so as I was preparing to speak this afternoon, I reflected on the image that this theme gives me.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: And the image that comes to my mind is one of a relay. Can you all picture the image of a relay race? Imagine a relay race where a button or a baton or a stick or a torch, in this case, is being passed from one runner to another. That is the image that came to my mind.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: Except that this was not about just a stick or literally a torch. It's about responsibility. It is an image of a seamless process, of a transition, actually.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: A transition of passing that baton or torch from one who is the runner to the receiver. But it also gave me an image of a privilege. Because imagine the elite athletes running in the relay, the privileged position that they are in.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: To be selected, to be on that relay team, you have to be the best. I reflected on the preparation process that those elite runners must go through for pre-qualification. I reflected on how many are left behind for so few to be selected to be in the race.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: As I thought about passing the torch and the relay race, I also reflected on the amount of training that one must go through to prepare for the race. Training in a safe place where you are free and allowed to make mistakes, to fail, to test yourself so that you can recover, improve, and get better. As I thought about this race, I reflected on the trust.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: The trust that you must gain. Not only to those selecting you to participate in the race, but the trust that you must gain from those that you are with in the race. It occurred to me that this must be a trust generated over time.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: Starting in small races, winning, running, improving, failing, improving, getting better, and qualifying for the big race. I reflected on the significance of being in that race. The stakes must be high when you are in such a race.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: Because, think about it, when you drop the torch, when you drop the baton, you are out of the race. So it's risky. The stakes are high.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: To be in the race, your hand must be steady, strong, fully grown, and fit to handle the torch, the baton. Steady enough to keep it across the race up to the end. Yet, I also realized that it must be teamwork.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: Because you cannot run in this race alone. The running passer, the one holding the torch, the baton, if you follow me on the image of this relay race, I want to keep you with me. The one who is concluding the path of the race, at that moment of transition, runs for a fair amount of time with the next one.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: Almost at the same speed, increasingly reducing as the new runner picks up the speed and holds steady of the baton or the torch. The newest runner is always faster, steadier, fresh, wealthy, just concluded runner, recedes, reduces, eventually stops. That is the image of our theme that came to mind as I was thinking of this talk this afternoon.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: But I also thought about what happens at that intersection moment. The amount of trust, relationship that exists between the concluding runner and the beginning one. The smooth handover that happens, almost like a dance on the floor.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: You have seen when the catching runner is putting the hand back behind themselves, not even looking. Trusting that the one behind them will pass it on in the right place at the right time, while they rest together, and the other gaining speed and firmness and confidence. I reflected on what happened at the end.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: At the end of the race, the finishing runner captures the emotion of the spectators, the audience. He or she is the winner. She is the hero.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: And is celebrated. But I also asked myself, is she really the hero? Is she really the winner? Who actually won the race? That is the question that keeps ringing in my mind as I think about passing the torch. Because while there is always the current, the moment that is fresh, that is celebrated, that is in the arena, that is on the podium.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: For every single moment, there is a past. But there is also a future. And so, for this theme regarding passing the torch, it doesn't mean that one generation almost drops off the scene out of the moment, while the other comes on the scene.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: But rather, it means that you have generations working together, sharing the abilities of the past, their capabilities, with the new ones. While asking each other why, regarding their entrenched beliefs, and refining their inherited values, so that they can build a stronger future together. It is about acknowledging that every present has got a past.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: And that every present has got a future, when it will be the past. I want us to reflect on what happens once you are in the relay race. This trust that I talked about is actually earned.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: It's not entitled. But it's also mutually expected. It goes all ways.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: Every race matters more than the previous one. Because you may have run many races, but eventually, when you are no longer competent to be in the race, you give way to the new runners to take the baton, and to take the torch. So, every new race increasingly becomes better, more significant, and more important than the previous one.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: You cannot claim trust, confidence from your past performances. It has got to be from your present and expected future. Likewise, citizens trust ethical leaders.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: Leaders who listen to them, represent them, and are accountable for their decisions. Leadership is a privilege. A privilege that comes with responsibilities.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: It cannot be an entitlement for benefit. But rather, leadership is a temporary trust that you earn, and hold, to serve, and live things better when your time comes to pass on the baton. Good leaders are ethical.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: But they are also authentic. I asked myself about this word, authentic. What would be the opposite of authentic? The word that kept coming to my mind is fake.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: So, if you don't want to be a fake leader, you learn to be an authentic leader. Authentic leaders earn trust through demonstrating ethical values, such as honesty, integrity, fairness, inclusion, and most importantly, delivering visible results to those that they serve. You may ask me, who gives permission to participate in the rest, or in the torch-passing business? I think earlier we had His Excellency President Paul Kagame mention that you don't have to ask anybody permission because it's your right.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: Passing on the torch, therefore, means that sometimes you must demand it. Demand it when you are authentic, and when you know that you are ready to hold and run with it. So, every generation has got a task to observe, to learn, and reflect, and also to articulate and ask themselves what it wants from their leaders.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: But you must be prepared to volunteer. Volunteer yourselves for the responsibilities that you seek to take. But let's be frank, it has not always been this smooth.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: Sometimes it has called for a generation to take on a fight. Yes, people have shed blood and lost lives in the process of demanding for change to happen. And so today, I want to propose that we write a new book.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: A book entitled, a book titled or called Passing the Torch. A book where young Africans are co-authors, not just readers or bystanders. If you agree with me, I would like to propose that this new book have five chapters and a conclusion.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: Let me suggest to you what, in my view, could be part of this book. What if chapter one of the book was about the process? That the process must start with honest conversation, like the one happening here today in Kigali. A conversation that calls for mutual respect.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: Respect for one another, the young, the old, the emerging leaders, and everybody in between. A chapter that would also cover a subject that reminds us that we exist and thrive on the sweat and blood of others who have been there before us. That has built many institutions that we have benefited from.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: Often under extremely hard conditions. A chapter that would recognize that those before us had their flaws. They were not perfect.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: But we are part of them. Because we are here because they were there. We have an obligation to learn and understand our history.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: Both the good and the bad alike. Consider our language, our culture, governance institutions, the security that we have enjoyed, the social and economic institutions we have inherited. All are a result of those who have been before us.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: They deserve our respect. Because we can only build on what they have done. Younger generations bring new tools.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: They bring new ways and new networks. And expectations on representation and accountability. But neither generation has all the answers.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: Because it's about the journey. Not the destination. It continues and continues and continues.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: I propose that chapter 2 would look at institutions. And suggest that institutions are the bridge that builds the bridge. I would suggest that institutions are the bridge that connects generations.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: That institutions are stewards of the past. And they are insurance for the future. The torch, in my earlier example, must represent the vision, a sense of direction, and the clarity of purpose with a destination that is clear and in sight.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: A nation's destiny is therefore reflected in its institutions. The capability of the people running them. And the common culture that guides their habits and behaviors.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: In this chapter, we would suggest that today's generation of leaders has the singular mission to redeem Africa's dignity. You see, the world all around us has prospered. While Africa remains stagnant and in many ways declining.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: Our continent, as a result, and its people, are humiliated on a regular basis. Disrespected and not taken seriously. Because of the poverty that we endure, the bad governance and misgovernance that our leaders have shown around the world.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: It's our responsibility to change this. I would suggest that chapter 3 of this new book would look at the intergenerational succession process. And conclude that it's determined by the mindset of our leaders.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: Their habits, their values, and behaviors and choices they make. And it would ask, are they ethical leaders? Ethical leadership is important because leaders model the institutions they lead and the people under their stewardship. While individuals inspire change, it's the institutions they form or build that sustain the change.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: So, passing the torch, therefore, must mean handing over not only the skills, but also the values and the institutional memory that our leaders before us have had. It also means that the new generation must govern more ethically and more authentically than their previous generation. I would suggest that chapter 4 of this book would have a case study.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: And this case study would be called the African School of Governance. The case study would suggest that a school like the African School of Governance must have as its mission to prepare and create a new generation of African leaders that are ethical, that have a commitment for the service of their people, and have the confidence in their identity as Africans and aspire to lead change in their communities. The case study would suggest that the African School of Governance should be a place where leaders aspire to walk the talk and model the leaders that Africa deserves.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: This case study should suggest that the African School of Governance is a school to shape the confidence of the African leaders and claim their place in the global community of nations. The last chapter of this book would look at a practical example. It would create a film, a movie, that illustrates the intergenerational dialogue required to have a smooth passing on the torch and intergenerational handover.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: In fact, shortly you will be watching that film. The film shows four Africans, two older ones and two younger ones, answering the same questions on leadership, on power and citizenship. And I will invite you to watch where the generations agree, meaning what to carry forward, and where they differ, meaning what to change or what to discard.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: The film is also a catalyst to ask ourselves two key questions. What must we carry forward from those who came before us? And what must we have the courage to leave behind or to change? This new book project has a conclusion. And the conclusion reminds us that the torch is not simply an object or something that we inherit and keep, but rather it's a responsibility.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: A responsibility whose value depends on what we do with it. How brightly we choose to keep it burning and alive. And whether we also prepare ourselves to carry it forward and ahead from us when the time comes.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: Thank you very much for your kind attention.

segments.speaker: Sharon Fru · Moderator
segments.text: Thank you so much. Thank you so much, Mr. Francis.

segments.speaker: Sharon Fru · Moderator
segments.text: I am really proud to be under your leadership. And from your remarks, I picked a lot of points, but then I would stress more on this. He mentioned that Passing the Torch is about generations learning from each other.

segments.speaker: Sharon Fru · Moderator
segments.text: And also he said about the book that has different chapters, including the process, institutions, mindset of our leaders. And I hope everybody also picks something that they think will apply in their lives. So thank you so much.

segments.speaker: Sharon Fru · Moderator
segments.text: And I would like to also take this moment to welcome Honorable Daniela Patricia de Almeida. Please forgive me if I don't pronounce the name well. She is the Secretary of State for Youth of the Republic of Angola.

segments.speaker: Sharon Fru · Moderator
segments.text: She's going to deliver her remarks. Please put your hands together as we welcome her. Thank you.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: Well, I'm not very tall, as you can see. Distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen, dear young leaders of Africa. It is a great privilege to be here today to reflect on a subject that is particularly close to my heart.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: The role of different generations in shaping the present and the future of our continent. As a young African, a young leader, and a member of government, I approach this conversation not only from an institutional perspective, but also from a deeply personal one. When we speak about civic action across generations, we are essentially speaking about identity, responsibility, commitment, and the legacy we wish to leave behind.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: When we speak about actions across generations, we are essentially speaking about identity. Every generation inherits a world it didn't create. But each generation has the responsibility to decide what kind of world it will leave behind.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: Across Africa, previous generations fought for independence, dignity, and the right for our people to determine their own destiny. Their courage, determination, and sacrifices laid the foundations upon which we stand today. Our generation has inherited those achievements, but also a new set of challenges and responsibilities.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: Today, our struggles take different forms. We are confronted with unemployment, inequality, social exclusion, and the need to create greater opportunities for our people. The challenges may have changed, but our responsibility remains the same.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: To leave Africa better than we found. I firmly believe that leadership must begin, first and foremost, with a profound sense of commitment to our countries, to our past, to our present, and to our future. We cannot contribute to the development of our countries without understanding their history, appreciating the journey, and recognizing the sacrifices of those who came before us.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: Understanding our past doesn't mean being bound by it. It means having the maturity to build upon its achievements, learn from its mistakes, and make better choices for the future. For me, patriotism is not simply about expressing love for one's country.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: It is about demonstrating that love through our actions, our integrity, our discipline, our willingness to contribute to the collective good. Throughout my journey, I have come to understand that leadership is not defined by the positions we occupy, the titles we hold, or the authority entrusted to us. Leadership is defined by what we do with that responsibility.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: Occupying a position of responsibility is not merely a privilege, it is, above all, a duty. As young leaders, our personal ambitions must never overshadow our collective responsibilities. The positions we occupy are temporary, but the impact of our decisions can extend far beyond our time in office.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: We must constantly ask ourselves, whose life has improved because of our responsibilities? However, the responsibility of transforming Africa is not exclusively to those who occupy positions of political leadership. Every young African, regardless of their profession, background, or circumstances, has a role to play in the development of our continent. As this is a message I particularly want to share with my fellow young Africans today, that whatever you choose to become in life, commit yourself to being the very best that you can be.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: If you're a doctor, then please strive to be the best doctor that you can be, because someone's life may depend on the quality of professional that you are. If you are a teacher, then please strive to become the best teacher that you can be, because the future of an entire generation may be influenced by the knowledge and the values that you transmit. If you're an engineer, a farmer, a public servant, then pursue excellence in everything that you do.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: And if you are a student, be the best that you can be. Take your education seriously, because your preparation for the responsibility of building Africa begins long before you enter the professional world. We do not all need to become politicians or occupy positions of power to transform our countries.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: We need to understand the importance of the role we already play and fulfill it with a profound sense of responsibility. Africa needs young people who are not only ambitious, but also committed. Young people who understand that personal success should not be disconnected from collective progress.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: We cannot aspire to build excellent institutions, strong economies, and prosperous societies if we are unwilling to demand excellence from ourselves. Our commitment to our countries must be reflected in the quality of our work, in our punctuality, in our discipline, in our integrity, and in the way we fulfill our responsibilities, even when no one is watching. Because the quality of professionals we become today will, to a great extent, determine the quality of the society we build tomorrow.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: Working closely with young people in Angola has reinforced many of these convictions that I have just shared with you. I have encountered young people with extraordinary talent, ambition, and resilience, whose circumstances have not always allowed them to realize their full potential. I have witnessed young people who were once involved in criminality find new directions in life through vocational training and access to opportunities.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: I have seen what happens when you choose to believe in young people whom society may have already given up on. I have witnessed young people with very strong will to win. We cannot contribute to the development of our country without understanding our history, like I have shared in the past.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: Just a second, because I forgot something very important that I would like to share with you. I'm very sorry, just a second. Technology.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: These experiences have taught me that when a young person is born, the neighborhood in which they grow up and the circumstances in which they are born should never determine how far they can go in life. Sometimes what stands between a young person and a completely different future is simply an opportunity. And for those of us who have been entrusted with the positions of responsibility, creating those opportunities must be a priority.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: While encouraging young people to work hard, pursue excellence, and assume responsibility for their future, we must also recognize our responsibility to create the conditions that allow them to succeed. In Angola, we have been strengthening programs that promote employability, technological innovation, quality education, and social inclusion, notably through youth development plan. With a strong emphasis on the active participation of young people.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: These efforts demonstrate sustainable development is most effective when built through partnership with government institutions, youth organizations, and international partners working together in that manner. Ultimately, our commitment must be to ensure that no young person is left behind. Another fundamental element of civic participation is trust.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: Trust between citizens and institutions. Trust between leaders and communities. And between generations.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: Trust cannot simply be demanded. It must be earned through consistency, through transparency, through accountability, and above all, actions. As public servants, we must be willing not only to speak to young people, but to listen to them as well.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: Listening doesn't always mean that we will always agree. It means recognizing that different perspectives are legitimate and that meaningful participation matters. Equally, civic responsibility doesn't mean an end with governments.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: It begins with each and everyone. It is reflected in how we treat communities, how we respond to injustice, how we respect our differences, and how we protect the public resources and how willing we are to contribute to the common good. Ladies and gentlemen, there is often a tendency to describe the relationship between generations through their differences.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: We may communicate differently, approach challenges differently, and even have different understandings on leadership and power. But beneath all of these differences, we often share the same fundamental aspirations. Dignity, prosperity, opportunity, and a better future for our people.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: Older generations bring experience. They bring wisdom, historical memory. Younger generations, on the other hand, bring creativity, innovation, new perspective, and the courage to question and establish new ways of doing things.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: However, dear young women and men of Africa, we need both. We must learn to disagree without becoming divided. To challenge without disrespecting one another.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: And to innovate without losing sight of who we are. The future of Africa must not be built on one generation alone, but through dialogue, mutual respect from one another, cooperation, and shared sense of purpose across generations. Dear young leaders of Africa, let us be a generation whose love for Africa is demonstrated not only through our words, not only through what we speak, but through our actions.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: Let us be remembered not simply as a generation that inherited achievements from the previous generations, but let us be remembered as a generation that had the courage, the competence, the discipline, and the commitment to take Africa further. The generation that came before us has done their job. They fought their battles, but they made many, many sacrifices and left us their legacy.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: Now it's our turn. What will the future generations say about us? And for that reason, I would like to ask every single young person in this room, what legacy are we willing to leave for the future generations of young leaders of Africa? So that's why I want to conclude and tell you that in Angola, we have an important saying. I come from the Ministry of Youth and Sports, and we always say that with young people, Angola will win.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: But today in this room, today in Rwanda, today in Kigali, this is the capital of the African youth, and today I say that with young people, Africa will win. And since we've been seated for quite a while, I would like you to help me to say these words, just to shake the room a bit this room. Can you please rise and stand up so we can say these words really loudly and proudly? With young people, Africa will win.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: I will talk with young people, and you will respond saying that Africa will win. With young people, Africa will win. With young people, Africa will win.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: With discipline, Africa will win. With capacitated young people, Africa will win. With patriotism, Africa will win.

segments.speaker: H.E. Danila Patrícia de Almeida Bragança · Secretary of State for Youth, Angola
segments.text: With commitment with our continent, Africa will win. Sorry, I can't hear you. With young people, Africa will win.

segments.text: Ladies and gentlemen, thank you very much. Thank you. I had a technical problem.

segments.speaker: Sharon Fru · Moderator
segments.text: Thank you so much, Honorable Ms. Patricia. Honestly, I was going to say that I'll be like you when I grow up, but I'm already old. So I can't say it again, but I'm actually going to learn from you.

segments.speaker: Sharon Fru · Moderator
segments.text: From your speech, I picked a lot of things, but I would like to mention three that are very important, and I think young people in the room can also learn from that. She said leadership is not a position, power, or authority that you have. It is what you do with that position or authority that you have.

segments.speaker: Sharon Fru · Moderator
segments.text: And I think that speaks to a lot of us in the room. And she also mentioned that our assignment right now as people of Africa is to leave our continent better than we actually found it. Yes, we all got that right.

segments.speaker: Sharon Fru · Moderator
segments.text: All right, thank you so much. And we're actually going to enter an exciting moment. I know we young people, we like movies, films, series, or whatever.

segments.speaker: Sharon Fru · Moderator
segments.text: So this is a very good moment for us to enjoy that. I would like to welcome the media team to help us watch Pass the Torch film. It's a short film that brings voices from across generations.
So we're going to learn from different perspectives, different experiences, and different young people and also old people. Thank you. My name is Elika Eljungi Birangira.
I am 11 years old. I was born on the 21st of July, 2015. My name is Mahmoud Salem.
I was born on the 1st of January, 1998. My name is Monique Nsanzabaganwa, and I was born in 1971. My name is Titor Terimera.
I was born in Igatsibo in 1944. My parents are good leaders. They are really nice and kind.
They lead with responsibility. I might have seen the leaders, they were calling them abattoirs. One was related to me, it was my uncle.

He was a man who was respected, and always people were coming to see him and surrounding him. My parents showed me how leadership is, and how they managed our house and they contributed to our community. My father, as I was growing up, was a teacher.

He was an educational leader. I remember in the morning, in between his taking the shower and dressing up to go to the office, he would have a long list of people lining up actually for signature, for this, for a problem being solved for that. So before actually he went to the office in the morning, he had already done his local community leader thing.
We educated our children. We had many who went to school. Before, our generation was not going to school.

My generation, we are getting or we are stabilizing Rwanda. I think they didn't consider the progress as a gift or as something that should happen. Our generation's role is for economic liberation of our continent.

Stop talking to problems or about problems, and try to be a part of solutions. How are you? How is your family? How was your family? All that now, we are now saying, I want to go to America. That is the wishes of young people now.
They want it to be, I want to go to Rwanda. When you have got a country, you owe it everything. Everything.
To be nice, to have responsibilities. When I see a plastic bottle on the floor, I can pick it up and put it in the trash. They do like this, or something like that.
Hello. Hello. Hello.
Clock? Clock it. Clock it what? Clock it what? At that point, I don't know. What does it mean? Something to eat? To clock it there? It means, clock it.
It smells like, wow. For example, if you see someone, you are so beautiful today, clock it. It smells like, wow, really, bravo.
Responsibility. Responsibility. Influence.
Hello. There is power in unity and co-creation. Because you never go solo.

Even if it's in your school project, you always are better off working with others. Please listen to us. We are not here to replace you, but to work with you, to benefit from you, to continue your journey.

segments.speaker: Sharon Fru · Moderator
segments.text: Put your hands together for the film, please. I am very sure you enjoyed it. Let's clap for all the people in this short movie, please.

segments.speaker: Sharon Fru · Moderator
segments.text: We have heard and we have seen four people, four generations, one Africa, and two questions to keep in mind. What will you carry forward? And what do you have the courage to leave behind? What are those things that are no longer serving our community that you are willing to leave behind? We should start thinking about those questions. But before that, let's see how we understand each other.
Just turn to your neighbor and demonstrate how you can say, call me. You guys, you saw it from the movie, that's why. I'm pretty sure some people didn't know.
But there are some people in the room who are not participating. How do you sign, call me? This is how I do it. I have another one.

I know Mr. Francis is actually the king of that one. Does everybody in the room understand what clock it means? Maybe Francis can stand up and show you how they actually do it. Yes, everybody clock it.
Thank you, Miriam. We want to appreciate every generation in the room. Alright, so we have another game.
It's not a game. We want to actually appreciate each and every generation represented in the room. I know that sometimes some people are shy of their age and maybe you don't want to look that old.

But this time around, we would like you to be honest so that we can take it as an opportunity to learn from your experience and the wisdom you bring to African continent. Alright, so if you were born before 1980, raise your hand. Clap for them, clap for them.
Thank you for being honest. You're actually the other generation we want to learn from. Thank you.
And if you were born before 1970, please stand up. If you were born before 1970, please stand up. Clap for them, but please stay standing.
Please stay standing if it's possible. So comrades, greeting comrades. And now it's time for our Gen Z leaders.

If you were born after 2000, please stand up. Actually, people who were born before 1970 were supposed to stay standing. Is it because you're old that I decided to sit down? People who were born after 2000.
I see a lot of young people there. If you were born before 2000, sorry, after 2000, please stand up. After 2000.

Guys, and the people who were born before 1970 were supposed actually to keep standing. I don't know why they decided to sit down. I don't know if it's because of age, but it is going to be very short.
So people who are seated, which category do you belong to? Reincarnation? I don't know. Alright, so thank you so much. If you look around, you see that we have a diverse community in the room.

We have a lot of people from different generations, different experiences, and different perspectives. So we are definitely here to learn from each other. Is that not why we are here, Miriam? Definitely.

Yes, we are not here to compete against each other. We are here to share those experiences, bring them into this room, and see how we can learn from one another to shape the Africa we want to see today and the Africa we want to see tomorrow too. Alright, so now we are going to go into discussions.

segments.speaker: Sharon Fru · Moderator
segments.text: But before that, let us hear from one of the young voices in the room. Ladies and gentlemen, please join me to welcome Prosper Singandi to the stage as he comes to share his reflections on this topic.

segments.speaker: Prosper Sangidi · Lead student, ASG
segments.text: Greetings, everyone.

segments.speaker: Prosper Sangidi · Lead student, ASG
segments.text: Please allow me to stand on top of the protocols that have been already observed. Before I start my reflections, I've been given five minutes and I've been told to mind my time. Allow me to shout out to my Zimbabweans.

segments.speaker: Prosper Sangidi · Lead student, ASG
segments.text: So, I am from Zimbabwe. Zimbabweans? Thank you, thank you. So, I have taken a few reflections to reflect on my understanding of passing the torch from what we have discussed so far.

segments.speaker: Prosper Sangidi · Lead student, ASG
segments.text: My understanding of passing the torch is, number one, it is a seamless transition. It has to be smooth. Number two, there is a training before the seamless transition for it to be a success.

segments.speaker: Prosper Sangidi · Lead student, ASG
segments.text: Number three, the transition is risky. Teamwork is needed to succeed and no one can do it alone. Now, in passing the torch between generations, questions are being raised by the youth.

segments.speaker: Prosper Sangidi · Lead student, ASG
segments.text: Should we be invited to the relay? If we are not to wait for an invitation, is the environment conducive enough for us to train and to fail and to learn? And finally, to join the race? Most importantly, is the older generation staying for guidance after they pass the torch? Ladies and gentlemen, I will leave you with these questions that require us to find answers together. Neither generation hears the answers alone. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Sharon Fru · Moderator
segments.text: Please, Prosper, I would like to repeat that question because we would like to start from it. Thank you. Everybody, please pay attention because you might want to answer or possibly give a reflection or a contribution.

segments.speaker: Prosper Sangidi · Lead student, ASG
segments.text: So, I will read the questions again. Should we be invited to the relay? If we are not to wait for an invitation, is the environment conducive enough for us to train, to fail and to learn? And finally, to join the race? Most importantly, is the older generation staying for guidance after they pass the torch? Thank you.

segments.speaker: Sharon Fru · Moderator
segments.text: Thank you so much and I think Mr. Francis is the right person to answer that question.

segments.speaker: Sharon Fru · Moderator
segments.text: Yashas, please help us get a mic in front from the first row. Thank you. Two questions.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: Is the environment conducive enough for the young generation to try, make mistakes, to fail, learn and get better? Now, the question is about the environment and, you know, it will never be perfect. We are all coming here from diverse backgrounds. So, the environment that you call yours is unique to you and the circumstances are specific to that unique environment.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: However, there are some general principles that will always apply. One, as a young leader, the training many times does not happen formally. It's not the kind that you see at the African School of Governance.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: That is formal training. A lot of leadership training happens informally. From being close to your elders, from identifying and being close to your mentors, from you, yourself, committing yourself, volunteering, making yourself available for service when an opportunity comes.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: When they say, who wants to do this? Are you the first to put your hand up and say, yes, I am. When an idea comes up and nobody is volunteering to do it and nobody has asked. I give a simple example in the context that I work in.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: If you are in a meeting and you are a young person and you realize nobody has been assigned to take notes. Are you going to keep quiet and pretend that everybody is taking notes? Or will you put your hand up and say, sorry, sorry, chair. Is it okay if I can take notes and circulate them after this meeting? I notice nobody has been assigned to take notes.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: That is an example of stepping in, exercising leadership when you don't have authority. When you don't have a position of leadership and when nobody has asked you. But you create space for yourself to begin to be a leader.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: Imagine when those meeting notes come out and they are drafted and they are not accurate or well written. You will be corrected and you will learn from that fast experience of taking notes from a major meeting. Every moment you are in on a daily basis is an opportunity for you as a young person to step in and create space for yourself to exercise leadership.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: To be noticed, to be trained when you make a mistake, to be mentored for growth and for you to become a contender for joining the relay. Without spending much time about the so-called environment, we as leaders create opportunities for ourselves by wanting to lead. Expressing a desire and a commitment to volunteer so that that is seen by your attitudes, by your behavior in front of your elders.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: Let's face it, you are not the only one. It's a competitive environment. How do you stand out? You don't stand out by being obnoxious and shouting so that you get noticed.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: No, you get noticed, you stand out by being available to serve, volunteering, exercising the opportunity to be present and to serve others. That's how I would answer that question. You have agency.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: It's not something going to be handed to you. Nobody is carrying an opportunity around looking for you everywhere and say, here, take it. No, you have to have agency in your own growth, in your own personal development as a leader.

segments.speaker: Hon. Francis Gatare · President, African School of Governance
segments.text: And you do that by being present, actively wanting to serve. And then being noticed and being picked, being given responsibility, challenged, you make mistakes, you learn from them, you grow, you get mentored, you become better. So that's how you emerge out of the crowd as a leader.

segments.speaker: Sharon Fru · Moderator
segments.text: Thank you. Let's do a special clap for our president. I'm going to teach you the clap.

segments.speaker: Sharon Fru · Moderator
segments.text: There are some people in the room that are going to teach you the clap. I want ASG students to stand up, please. Yes.

segments.speaker: Sharon Fru · Moderator
segments.text: I think somebody should hand you a mic. Okay. All right.

segments.speaker: Sharon Fru · Moderator
segments.text: Thank you so much. Thank you so much for that special clapping. Yeah, we are learning new things.

segments.text: Young people in the room, if you do not answer, I can see people by uniform. Possibly I will be coming to your group and then you will have to give me somebody to answer. You can just raise your hand and then we will send somebody to give you the microphone.

segments.speaker: Sharon Fru · Moderator
segments.text: Or should I repeat the question again? The person in the movie said, do not wait to be invited. Now the question is to the young people, are you waiting for somebody to invite you? If yes, who? There is a hand.
